XII.1.title: Overcome the self, return to ritual
XII.1.reflection: Yan Hui asks about ren. To overcome oneself and return to ritual is ren; if for one day one could do this, the world would turn to ren. It comes from oneself, not from others. The steps: do not look, listen, speak or move against ritual. Hui says he will try, slow as he is. This is perhaps the most discussed definition of ren in the book.
XII.1.question: Which of the four, looking, listening, speaking or moving, most often leads you astray?
XII.1.exercise: For one day, notice each time you are about to speak against what you think right, and pause.

XII.2.title: As if receiving a great guest
XII.2.reflection: To Zhonggong: when you go out, treat everyone as if receiving an important guest; employ people as if performing a great sacrifice; do not impose on others what you would not wish for yourself. Then there will be no resentment in the state or in the family. The rule of shu appears here without the word.
XII.2.question: Whom could you treat today as if they were a great guest?

XII.3.title: Slow to speak
XII.3.reflection: Sima Niu, said to be talkative, asks about ren: the humane are slow to speak. Is that all? When doing is hard, can speaking be easy? The answer fits the asker, as so often.
XII.3.question: What do you talk about easily that is hard to do?

XII.4.title: Without worry or fear
XII.4.reflection: Sima Niu asks about the junzi: he has no worry and no fear. Is that all? If you look within and find nothing to be ashamed of, what is there to worry about or fear? Freedom from anxiety follows from a clear conscience.
XII.4.question: What worry of yours would disappear if your conscience were clear about it?

XII.5.title: All within the four seas
XII.5.reflection: Sima Niu grieves that everyone has brothers but he. His brother Huan Tui was the man who tried to kill Confucius. Zixia consoles him: life and death are fated, wealth and rank lie with Heaven; if the junzi is respectful and courteous, all within the four seas are his brothers. Kinship is widened by conduct.
XII.5.question: Who has become a brother or sister to you, though not by birth?

XII.6.title: Slander that soaks in
XII.6.reflection: Zizhang asks about clear-sightedness. One whom slander that soaks in slowly and accusations that sting like a wound cannot move may be called clear-sighted, and far-seeing. The two dangers are the slow and the sudden.
XII.6.question: Which reaches you more easily, slow gossip or a sudden accusation?

XII.7.title: Food, arms, trust
XII.7.reflection: Government needs enough food, enough arms and the trust of the people. If one must go? Arms. If another? Food: death has always been with us, but without trust a state cannot stand. Good faith is placed above survival itself.
XII.7.question: In a group you belong to, what would be lost if trust failed, even with everything else in place?

XII.8.title: A tiger's hide
XII.8.reflection: Ji Zicheng says the junzi needs only substance; why culture? Zigong answers: a team of horses cannot overtake the tongue. Culture is as important as substance; a tiger's hide with the hair removed is like a dog's. The pattern is part of what the thing is.
XII.8.question: What in you is only visible through its form?

XII.9.title: The tithe
XII.9.reflection: Duke Ai complains of a bad year and not enough revenue. Youzi suggests taxing a tenth. I take two tenths and it is not enough. If the people have enough, how can the ruler lack? If they lack, how can he have enough? The ruler's welfare depends on the people's.
XII.9.question: Where would taking less produce more in the end?

XII.10.title: Wishing life and death
XII.10.reflection: Exalt virtue by putting loyalty and good faith first and moving toward what is right. Confusion is to wish someone to live when you love them and to die when you hate them, both at once. The last line, a stray quotation from an ode, is out of place and probably belongs elsewhere.
XII.10.question: Is there someone toward whom your feelings swing from one extreme to the other?

XII.11.title: Ruler ruler, father father
XII.11.reflection: Duke Jing of Qi asks about government. Let the ruler be a ruler, the minister a minister, the father a father, the son a son. The Duke agrees: otherwise, even with grain, could I eat it? Each role must live up to its name. It is setting names right, zhengming, in four pairs.
XII.11.question: Which of your roles do you live up to least?

XII.12.title: Half a word
XII.12.reflection: Zilu could settle a dispute with half a word; he never slept on a promise. Decisiveness and reliability, the virtues of the impulsive disciple.
XII.12.question: What promise have you been sleeping on?

XII.13.title: No lawsuits
XII.13.reflection: In hearing lawsuits I am like anyone else; what is needed is that there be no lawsuits. Good government prevents disputes rather than judging them well.
XII.13.question: What dispute could you prevent rather than win?

XII.14.title: Without tiring
XII.14.reflection: Zizhang asks about government: keep at it without tiring, and carry it out with loyalty. Persistence and devotion, nothing more elaborate.
XII.14.question: What responsibility have you grown tired of?

XII.15.title: Learning held by ritual, again
XII.15.reflection: VI.25 returns without the word junzi: study widely in culture, draw it together with ritual, and one will not stray. The repetition shows how the book was gathered from overlapping sources.
XII.15.question: What draws your learning together?

XII.16.title: Helping the good in others
XII.16.reflection: The junzi helps others complete what is good in them and not what is bad; the small man does the opposite. Encouragement can point both ways.
XII.16.question: Whose good qualities could you help complete?

XII.17.title: To govern is to correct
XII.17.reflection: Ji Kangzi asks about government. To govern, zheng, is to correct, zheng, a pun in Chinese. If you lead by being correct, who will dare not to be? The ruler is again sent back to himself.
XII.17.question: What would you need to correct in yourself first?

XII.18.title: Thieves and desire
XII.18.reflection: Ji Kangzi worries about thieves. If you yourself did not desire, they would not steal even if you rewarded them. The Ji family had taken power and wealth from the ducal house. The answer is pointed.
XII.18.question: What disorder around you mirrors a desire of your own?

XII.19.title: Wind and grass
XII.19.reflection: Ji Kangzi asks about killing the bad to help the good. Why kill? Desire the good and the people will be good. The virtue of the junzi is wind, that of the small man grass; when the wind blows, the grass bends. The image rejects violence as a tool of government.
XII.19.question: Over whom are you the wind, and which way are you blowing?

XII.20.title: Distinction and notoriety
XII.20.reflection: Zizhang wants to be distinguished, which he defines as being known everywhere. That is notoriety, not distinction. The distinguished person is straight, loves what is right, weighs others' words and faces and puts himself below them. The notorious person puts on the look of ren and acts against it, without a doubt about himself.
XII.20.question: Do you want to be known, or to be worth knowing?

XII.21.title: Under the rain altars
XII.21.reflection: Walking with the Master among the rain altars, Fan Chi asks how to exalt virtue, correct hidden faults and resolve confusion. Good question! Put the work first and the reward after; attack your own faults, not others'; and in a moment's anger to forget yourself and your parents, is that not confusion?
XII.21.question: When did a moment's anger make you forget what mattered more?

XII.22.title: Love people, know people
XII.22.reflection: Fan Chi asks about ren: love people. About knowledge: know people. He does not understand, and Confucius adds: raise the straight above the crooked and the crooked will be straightened. Zixia later explains with the example of the sage kings, who raised one good minister and wrongdoers vanished. Love and knowledge are both turned outward, toward others.
XII.22.question: Whom do you know well enough to judge rightly?

XII.23.title: Advise a friend, then stop
XII.23.reflection: Zigong asks about friends. Advise them faithfully and guide them well; if that fails, stop, and do not shame yourself. Friendship has its own measure of correction, as IV.26 also said.
XII.23.question: With which friend should you stop advising?

XII.24.title: Friends through culture
XII.24.reflection: Master Zeng: the junzi gathers friends through culture and through friends supports his ren. Friendship is both formed by shared learning and a help to goodness.
XII.24.question: Which of your friendships began in something you studied or loved together?
